newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Dlr/yen risk reversals steepen, vols bid.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Dlr/yen risk reversals steepen, vols bid.

text.p: The persistent pricing skew for downside strike prices in dollar/yen options steepened further on Monday after the dollar tumbled to the 112-yen area overnight and offers for yen calls evaporated, traders said.

Risk reversals, the cost of swapping equally low-delta puts and calls, widened their already hefty skew for yen calls to levels unheard of in recent memory as the market braced for a further dollar slide, they said.
"The market's been very thin, dealers' books were already lopsided and we got this drop in the dollar," said Masao Okada, chief options dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.

One-month 25-delta dollar/yen risk reversal was quoted at 3.0/3.3 percentage points in late U.S. morning trade, with a deal at 3.0 reported after the dollar tumbled to an overnight low of 111.98 yen from Friday's close above 114 yen.
The one-month 25-delta had been trading mostly in the 2.0-2.75 point range in recent weeks. Until a few months ago, a 1.0-point slant was considered very sharp.

"Premium on the downside in dollar/yen has become so expensive," said MaryBeth Slack, FX options analyst at MCM OptionWatch. "The market is feeling very skeptical about these prices -- there's not a lot of trade going on."
Okada said the market had become so thin since just before the July 4 U.S. holiday that even the major market-making banks were asking for quotes on direct-dealing screens.
Still, traders said demand for downside strikes remained strong from end-users and bank dealers who had become short in downside gamma as a result of end-user buying.

Okada said many professional traders were opting for yen calls rather than shorting the dollar outright because, despite the market's overwhelmingly bearish sentiment on the dollar, spot in recent weeks had not fallen much and many dollar shorts had been squeezed by its frequent rebounds.
Implied volatilities also were generally bid up in dollar/yen. One-month at-the-money volatility rose to 12.4/12.6 percent from Friday's 10.7/11.1.
The volatility curve was slightly inverted, as gamma-rich shorter-dates were the most in demand. Three-month was quoted at 11.4/11.6 percent and one-year at 11.0/11.2.

By contrast, dollar/mark volatilities were only mildy firmer as the dollar stayed below last week's 1.7590-mark high, pulling back early and then bouncing back above 1.7500 marks toward U.S. midsession. One-month volatility was up a quarter point at 8.0/8.3 percent.
Sterling/mark volatilities were also firmer as spot hovered just below last week's 2.9650-mark high.
Slack said sterling's early pullback today seemed to be a mere consolidation after last week's rally, and a further upside probe was likely soon.
She noted some interest in mark puts at a strike price of 3.0 marks.
